section_summary: This section concludes a critical study of the conservative Co-Operative Democratic Party and contains a detailed GHQ study of the Japan Communist Party’s history, leadership, organization, finances, agrarian and labor programs, united-front strategy, platform, and draft constitution. It also includes a fortnightly survey of party alignments and constitutional debate, together with a biographical memorandum on Progressive Party leader Inukai Ken. The final pages begin another fortnightly report covering the Shinsei-kai, Communist speaking rights, constitutional wording, and divisions within the Liberal Party.

subfiles.title: Enclosure 2 to Despatch No. 519: Study of the Co-Operative Democratic Party
subfiles.about: The concluding portion evaluates the personnel, agrarian base, ideology, and political methods of the Co-Operative Democratic Party.
subfiles.summary: Study portraying the Co-Operative Democratic Party as agrarian, landowner-based and the right wing of Japanese politics, using progressive language for traditional ideas, though not clearly fascist.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 529: Study of the Japan Communist Party
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch transmits Harry Emerson Wildes’s study of the Japan Communist Party.
subfiles.summary: Despatch forwarding a July 24 GHQ study of the Japan Communist Party's leaders, policies, finances and draft constitution.

subfiles.title: Communist Party (Kyosanto)
subfiles.from: Harry Emerson Wildes, Government Section, GHQ/SCAP
subfiles.about: A comprehensive study examines the history, leadership, organization, tactics, constituencies, finances, platform, and constitutional proposals of the Japan Communist Party.
subfiles.summary: The study traces the party from its 1922 foundation and years of repression through its post-surrender reemergence, contrasting the confrontational Shiga-Tokuda approach with Nosaka Sanzo’s moderate parliamentary strategy. It profiles the Central Committee, election results, agrarian and labor programs, failed united-front campaign, mass meetings, internal discipline, finances, youth league, and women’s section. The author argues that the published platform and constitutional outline are deliberately vague and milder than the party’s probable long-term objectives. Particular attention is given to abolition of the Emperor system, land redistribution, labor organization, a proposed people’s republic, and the party’s effort to become acceptable to Japanese voters.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 543: Report by Dr. Wildes—Political Parties
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards Wildes’s report on Japanese political parties during July 1–15, 1946.
subfiles.summary: Despatch transmitting the GHQ study Political Parties 1-15 July 1946, with regular reports possible.

subfiles.title: Political Parties, 1–15 July 1946
subfiles.about: The memorandum surveys party consolidation, constitutional debate, democratization of party management, and the Social Democrats’ rejection of Communist collaboration.
subfiles.summary: Wildes reports that the proliferation of parties after the April election was giving way to five principal blocs, including a prospective New Party formed from smaller groups and independents. He reviews party positions on the draft constitution, emphasizing Inukai Ken’s privately submitted Progressive proposals and the Communists’ outline for a people’s republic. The memorandum also describes efforts by younger Liberal, Progressive, and Social Democratic politicians to decentralize party management, the discipline imposed on Osawa Hisashi, and the Social Democrats’ rejection of a Communist-sponsored democratic front.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 546: Report on Inukai Ken
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards a Government Section report on Progressive Party chief Inukai Ken.
subfiles.summary: Despatch transmitting a GHQ Government Section report on Inukai Ken, fifty-year-old chief of the Progressive Party.

subfiles.title: Inukai Ken
subfiles.about: A political biography analyzes Inukai Ken’s character, family background, intellectual formation, career, patrons, and political prospects.
subfiles.summary: Wildes portrays Inukai as a passive, philosophically inclined politician shaped first by his father, former prime minister Inukai Tsuyoshi, and later by Baron Shidehara Kijuro. The memorandum traces his university interests, marriage, admiration for China, Diet career, work connected with the Nanjing regime and China peace negotiations, and growing attraction to Catholic example. It argues that his influence rests chiefly on inherited prestige and political sponsorship, while noting his cultivation of new Diet members and the possible emergence of an Inukai bloc. The report regards his general influence as conservative but democratic and favorable to good relations with China and the West.

subfiles.title: Political Party Fortnightly Report, 16–31 July 1946
subfiles.about: The opening of the report reviews internal party disputes, the Shinsei-kai, Communist speaking rights, constitutional wording, and the Liberal Party split.
subfiles.summary: The report describes the Shinsei-kai as a coalition formed for Diet privileges, reviews debate on the Emperor as head or symbol of state, and discusses the fragmented Liberal Party. Continues beyond this section.
